Nose Jewels
NOHZ JOO-elz
noun
Rendering Hebrew nizmē hā’aph, “rings of the nose”; the nose-ring given to Rebekah as a bridal pledge and inventoried on the daughters of Zion.

Biblical Definition

The nose jewels close Isaiah’s third line of finery: “The rings, and nose jewels” (Isa 3:21). And like the earring, this ornament has an honorable twin. When Abraham’s servant found Rebekah at the well, “I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands” (Gen 24:47) — the word is the nose-ring, set on her face as the pledge of a bridegroom she had not yet seen. The LORD Himself takes up the image for His covenant with Jerusalem: “And I put a jewel on thy forehead, and earrings in thine ears, and a beautiful crown upon thine head” (Eze 16:12) — He decked her; the ornament was His love-token. That is what makes Isaiah 3 so heavy. The daughters wearing nose jewels in the inventory are wearing the very shape of bridal belonging — but self-bestowed, paraded for the street, tokens of no one’s pledge but their own vanity. An engagement ring with no bridegroom behind it is not romance but costume. Let the believer wear only what love has actually given. The ornaments that survive the day of seizure are the bestowed ones — grace tokens from the Bridegroom’s own hand — and the Church’s jewels are exactly that: “as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels” (Isa 61:10), every one of them His gift.

Webster 1828 Definition

The bridal nose-ring — Rebekah’s pledge and the LORD’s own love-token in Ezekiel — worn self-bestowed in Isaiah’s inventory: costume without a covenant.

NOSE JEWELS, rings of the nose; Hebrew nizmē hā’aph.

Set on Rebekah’s face as the pledge of an unseen bridegroom (Gen 24:47).

The LORD’s own image for decking covenant Jerusalem (Eze 16:12).

Inventoried on Zion’s daughters as self-bestowed finery (Isa 3:21).

An engagement ring with no bridegroom behind it is costume, not covenant.

Key Scripture

Isa 3:21 — "The rings, and nose jewels,"

Gen 24:47 — "And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter art thou? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands."

Eze 16:12 — "And I put a jewel on thy forehead, and earrings in thine ears, and a beautiful crown upon thine head."

Isa 61:10 — "I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels."

Modern Corruption

Bridal tokens worn without a bridegroom: the age dresses in the shapes of covenant belonging — self-bestowed — and calls the costume freedom.

expand to see more

The corruption is covenant-shaped costume. The nose jewel meant a pledge received; Zion’s daughters wore the shape of belonging while belonging to no one but themselves. The age repeats it at scale — the language and dress of devotion kept, the Bridegroom dismissed, intimacy’s tokens worn as trophies of autonomy.

The recovered principle is bestowed adornment. Ezekiel’s LORD decks His bride with His own hand, and Isaiah’s bride rejoices in jewels that are entirely gift. The believer wears only what love has actually given — grace-tokens, not self-purchased props — and such ornaments are the only ones the day of seizure cannot touch.

Hebrew Roots

Rendering the Hebrew “rings of the nose,” nose jewels are bridal pledges — honorable when bestowed, inventoried when self-worn without a bridegroom.
